https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, David McBride pleaded guilty to leaking military secrets to the media in 2023 By Lana Lam Sydney Published 4 hours ago A whistleblower jailed for leaking military secrets about Australia's involvement in Afghanistan has been released on parole after serving 27 months. In 2024, David McBride was sentenced to five years and eight months after pleading guilty to stealing top secret defence documents and giving it to the media. His actions later led to a landmark inquiry that found evidence that Australian forces had unlawfully killed 39 Afghans during the war. On Thursday, a spokesperson for the Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said McBride's "parole was considered and granted". The ex-military lawyer, who is being treated for lung cancer, will serve the rest of his sentence in the community under supervision. Shortly after the decision, advocacy group The Information Rights Project released a statement on McBride's behalf, according to national broadcaster ABC. He thanked his family "who never gave up on me and whose fighting spirit, love and humour inspired me every day" and praised "all my amazing supporters from around both Australia and the world who sent me such inspirational messages". McBride also revealed that he had been diagnosed with treatable lung cancer and would be having surgery to remove part of his lung. His lawyer Edwina Lloyd described the decision to grant his parole as "the right one", in a statement according to the ABC. She said McBride's life has been "defined by service to Australia", both as a legal officer for the Australian Defence Forces (ADF) and having served time for his crimes. During his court case , prosecutors argued that McBride's actions had been motivated by "personal vindication", and that the way he gathered, stored and then leaked the documents endangered Australia's national security and foreign policy. But McBride's lawyers asked for leniency, saying he shared the information with "honourable" intentions and out of a sense of personal duty. In sentencing McBride, the judge said while he was of "good character", sharing military secrets was a "gross breach of trust" and he had shown "no contrition" for his actions. The material he leaked to the ABC underpinned a series of reports in 2017 called The Afghan Files which provided unprecedented insight into Australia's elite special forces in Afghanistan, including allegations of war crimes. In 2020, the Brereton Report found "credible evidence" that elite soldiers have unlawfully killed 39 people. A special watchdog - the Office of the Special Investigator - was set up to look into the actions of 19 ADF members. Of its 53 cases, 39 have been finalised and two former Special Air Service (SAS) soldiers have been charged. Ben Roberts-Smith , Australia's most decorated living soldier, is facing five counts of the war crime of murder after he was charged earlier this year, while Oliver Schulz faces one count of the same charge. Photograph: Parth Desai/AP Arizona At least 15 people may be missing after flash flood in Arizona’s Grand Canyon Dozens evacuated after flash-flood event near Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch, officials say Coral Murphy Marcos and agencies Sun 30 Aug 2026 20.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 20.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 15 people may be missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon national park in Arizona on Saturday afternoon, according to the National Park Service. The flash-flood event occurred in the area of Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch, where park staff and the Arizona department of public safety have evacuated more than 60 people as of Sunday morning. No injuries have been reported as of Sunday, according to a statement from the National Park Service. Flooding devastated swathes of Indiana but response is hampered by politics Read more “Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch Canteen and cabins, and the entire North Kaibab Trail from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch are closed until further notice,” the statement said. Park officials announced the number of people who remain missing or unaccounted for in a separate statement , requesting the public to notify the government agency of information they may know about “hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor” on Saturday, as well as “anyone who had a campground reservation in the affected corridor”. Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, officials said, and the Colorado River is closed to river traffic until further notice as metal structures and debris enter the river. About half an inch to 1in (1-2.5cm) of rain fell within about 30 minutes in the rocky area where there is a steep drop in elevation, Justin Johndrow, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Flagstaff, told the Associated Press. View image in fullscreen Handout image released by the Grand Canyon National Park Service shows remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek. Photograph: J Thompson, handout/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images “Most of it ran off instantly,” Johndrow said. He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping about 6,000ft (1,800 meters). More rain and thunderstorms were possible in the area into Monday.
